detailed_rationale:
NCC Limited is a diversified EPC/construction major (buildings, water, electrical, roads, irrigation). Its order book grew a healthy 16% YoY to Rs 83,004cr - roughly 4x annual revenue - which on paper gives strong multi-year visibility, and Q4 FY26 showed a sequential recovery (revenue up to Rs 6,233cr from Rs 4,868cr in Q3, net profit up 60% sequentially to Rs 216.8cr). But the year-over-year and full-year trend is the more telling signal: FY26 consolidated revenue actually declined ~6% to ~Rs 20,823cr (matching the quant feed's -6.2% revenue_growth_1y) 'due to sector-wide funding stress' per one tracker, and Q4 FY26 net profit fell 18% YoY (Rs 216.8cr vs Rs 265.1cr in Q4 FY25) despite the larger order book. Trackers attribute the margin pressure to payment delays from clients, rising input costs (including West Asia-crisis-linked commodity/logistics inflation) and general execution slowdown - i.e., the backlog exists on paper, but converting it into revenue and profit at the previously-assumed margin has gotten harder this year, not easier.

The quant scorecard reflects this tension precisely: growth_3y_score is a healthy 41.2 (built on the prior 10.2% 3-year revenue CAGR, before this year's decline), but growth_1y_score has collapsed to just 6.6, and - unusually for this batch - both the 3-year and 1-year recommendation windows land on Sell (final_score_3y 30.4, final_score_1y 27.5). Quality score is modest (34.8) and the balance sheet is reasonably conservative (D/E 0.44, interest coverage 2.46x), so this is not a leverage-distress story; it is an execution and working-capital story. The stock is statistically cheap (PE ~13x, value_score 69.3), which is typical for EPC contractors carrying large but slow-converting order books, but cheapness alone does not offset the fact that the most recent, most decision-relevant trend - actual revenue and profit delivery - is moving the wrong way.
recommendation_rationale: A large and growing order book is a genuine positive, but it is a claim on future execution, not delivered performance - and the delivered performance this year (revenue -6%, Q4 profit -18% YoY despite a sequential bounce) shows real margin and working-capital pressure from payment delays and cost inflation. With both the 3-year and 1-year quant windows independently landing on Sell, and no offsetting balance-sheet distress story that a rescue argument would need to counter, we see this as a straightforward Sell rather than a rescue candidate - the backlog is a reason to watch for a turn, not a reason to hold through the current execution slippage.
summary: NCC has a large and growing order book, but this year's actual results moved in the wrong direction - revenue declined and profit fell year-on-year on payment delays and rising costs, even as the company points to a strong pipeline for the future. Until execution and margins actually turn, we would not read the backlog alone as a reason to hold, and recommend Sell.
positive_para: The order book of Rs 83,004cr (+16% YoY, ~4x revenue) gives NCC genuine multi-year revenue visibility if execution normalises, and the balance sheet is conservatively run (D/E 0.44, interest coverage ~2.5x) with a sequential profit recovery visible in Q4. The stock is inexpensive on conventional multiples (PE ~13x).
negative_para: The headline backlog has not translated into delivered growth this year: FY26 revenue fell ~6% and Q4 profit dropped 18% YoY on payment delays from clients and rising input/logistics costs, and the 1-year growth score has collapsed to 6.6/100 even as the 3-year score still reflects the pre-slowdown trend. EPC execution risk (client payment delays, commodity cost overruns, working-capital strain) is a real and recurring feature of this sector, and there is no clear evidence yet that this cycle has turned.
reverse_dcf_judgment: At ~13x trailing earnings the multiple already discounts EPC-sector execution risk, but it still assumes the order book converts to revenue and margins recover from this year's dip. Given payment delays and cost inflation are ongoing rather than resolved, the multiple is fair for a business proving it can execute its backlog - not yet a bargain. Judgment: fair, contingent on an execution turn that has not yet shown up in the numbers.
